There is a country that no mapmaker has bothered to chart. You enter it every night, and no one asks for a passport. The sky there is not a sky but a held breath, gray and slightly warm, and the ground beneath your feet feels more like the inside of a cupped hand than soil.

You are not you in this country. You are the person who was you before the first memory that defines you — almost no one. You are the shape of a thought that hasn't decided what to be yet. You stand in that in-between, that thin blue second where the last film of dream is still developing in one eye and the first pixel of morning hasn't struck the other, and you realize you've never actually experienced the space between. You've just been teleported.

Something about the architecture of the night — the way the curtains of sleep fold like wet paper — makes the impossible feel ordinary. You've walked this country a thousand times. You know you'll wake soon. You know the kitchen will be too bright and your hands will feel like gloves and the world will snap back into its heavy, defined edges.

But for now, in the country between, nothing has edges. You can stand in the middle of nowhere and feel, wordlessly, that you are exactly where you're supposed to be, and that the next breath is a gift no one is keeping score on.

Then the kettle in your kitchen hums. You're gone.
